title: AFF Basics: The Affirmative Core
subtitle: Stock Issues · Mission 04
tagline: Every year, the whole country picks {{cyan:one}} big problem. As the {{amber:Affirmative}}, you have to prove four things to win — or your case falls apart.

slides.headline: WELCOME TO THE BRIDGE, CADETS
body: Think about something in the world right now that feels {{amber: unfair}} to you. A rule, a system, a problem nobody seems to be fixing.
Every year, the entire country of policy debaters picks {{amber: one}} of those problems and argues about how to fix it. That topic is called the `resolution`.

If you debate `Affirmative`, your mission is to convince the judge that the resolution is a {{cyan: great idea}}. But you can't just say so — you have to prove **four specific things**, or your whole case fails.
Today you learn what those four things are. Log in with your Debate Partner. Let's launch.

items.label: Explain the {{cyan: resolution}} in your own words
Know why every {{cyan: AFF}} case needs a {{amber: Plan}}

slides.definition: The `resolution` is the {{cyan:single topic statement}} the Affirmative team must support and the Negative team must argue against — picked once a year for the whole country.
slides.plainWords: It's the mission statement for the entire debate season. One sentence. Everyone debates it. You'll argue *both* sides at tournaments.
slides.analogy: Think of it like a galaxy-wide directive: one objective, two teams, every round. The {{cyan: AFF}} says *"yes, this is a great idea."* The {{amber: NEG}} says *"no, this will not work or is a bad idea."*

slides.headline: S.H.I.S. — THE AFFIRMATIVE BURDEN
slides.intro: An Affirmative case is like a pizza: dough, sauce, cheese, toppings. Forget the dough and you don't have a pizza — you have a mess. In debate, if you miss even **one** of these four `stock issues`, your whole mission fails. We call them {{amber:S.H.I.S.}}

cards.name: SIGNIFICANCE
cards.description: {{cyan:The Scale.}} You can't ask the whole country to change its rules for a tiny problem. Prove the problem is **massive** — millions of people, billions of dollars, something big.

cards.name: HARMS
cards.description: {{amber:The Damage.}} Identify exactly what bad things are happening **right now** because of the problem. Real people, real damage.

cards.name: INHERENCY
cards.description: {{cyan:The Barrier.}} If the problem is so big and harmful, why hasn't someone fixed it yet? Prove the current system is *stuck* and cannot fix itself.

cards.name: SOLVENCY
cards.description: {{amber:The Cure.}} It's not enough to complain about a problem. Prove that your specific `plan` will actually **repair the damage**.

slides.definition: The `plan` is the Affirmative's {{cyan:specific, concrete policy proposal}} to fix the harms. Without a plan, you're just complaining about a problem — you don't have a debate case.
slides.plainWords: It's your blueprint. A winning Commander always brings one. It answers four questions: *who* does it, *what* exactly they do, *how* it's paid for, and *when* it starts.
slides.analogy: Think of an architect drawing up plans for a building. You wouldn't hire a contractor who just shouted *"the old building is bad!"* and showed up with no blueprint. Same in debate.

slides.headline: THE BLUEPRINT: WRITING YOUR PLAN
slides.intro: Every solid Affirmative plan answers four questions. Miss one and the {{amber: NEG}} will hammer you for it.

rows.name: AGENT — Who will do it?
rows.description: Name the actor with the power to actually carry out your plan: Congress, the Supreme Court, the EPA, the United Nations. Be specific.

counter.label: WATCH OUT
counter.text: *"The government"* is too vague. Which branch? Which agency?

rows.name: ACTION — What exactly will they do?
rows.description: Spell out the policy in plain language. Pass this law. Ban this thing. Fund this program. One clear sentence beats five fuzzy ones.

counter.label: WATCH OUT
counter.text: Vague verbs like *"address"* or *"improve"* leave the NEG room to misread your plan.

rows.name: FUNDING — How will we pay for it?
rows.description: Even a great plan needs a wallet. Existing budgets, new taxes, redirected military spending — pick one and own it.

counter.label: WATCH OUT
counter.text: *"It pays for itself"* is a claim. You'll need a {{cyan: warrant}} for that.

rows.name: TIMELINE — When does it start?
rows.description: Immediately on passage? In phases over five years? The timeline shapes whether the plan can actually achieve `solvency`.

counter.label: WATCH OUT
counter.text: A plan that *"starts someday"* solves *"nothing today."*

prompt.label: SYSTEM CHECK
prompt.scenario: The four stock issues each answer a different `core question`. Match each one to the question it answers.
prompt.question: Match each stock issue to its core question.

items.text: Who is getting hurt right now?

correct.title: ✓ TARGET ACQUIRED
body: All four locked in. {{cyan:S.H.I.S.}} isn't a random list — each one fills a different job in your case.
**Significance** sizes it up. **Harms** names who suffers. **Inherency** explains why it's stuck. **Solvency** proves your fix works.
correct.followup: Memorize the acronym: S-H-I-S. You'll use it every round you debate Affirmative.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ MISFIRE — RECALIBRATE
body: Close, but not all four lined up. The trickiest one to keep straight is usually `inherency` — it asks *"why hasn't this been fixed already?"* not *"how do we fix it?"* (that's `solvency`).
Try the matching again with that distinction in mind.

prompt.label: INHERENCY CHECK
prompt.scenario: Your Affirmative case argues the U.S. should ban a certain pesticide. The NEG stands up and says: *"The EPA is already phasing out that pesticide next year."*
prompt.question: Which stock issue is the NEG attacking?

options.text: Significance — they're saying the problem is too small
Harms — they're saying nobody is actually being hurt
Inherency — they're saying the problem is already getting fixed
Solvency — they're saying our plan won't work

correct.title: ✓ TARGET ACQUIRED
body: Exactly. `Inherency` asks *"why hasn't this been fixed already?"* If the NEG can show the system is **already fixing it** without your plan, your inherency collapses and there's nothing left for your plan to do.
Your counter: prove the EPA's phase-out is too slow, too narrow, or won't actually finish — that the barrier is still there.
correct.followup: Inherency is the trickiest stock issue. Half of NEG strategy lives here.

a.title: ✕ MISFIRE
body: Significance is about the **size** of the problem (*"this is too small to matter"*). The NEG isn't saying the pesticide problem is small — they're saying it's **already being handled**. That's `inherency`.

b.title: ✕ MISFIRE
body: Harms attacks *who is getting hurt right now*. The NEG didn't deny anyone's getting hurt — they said the system is **already fixing it**. That's `inherency`.

d.title: ✕ MISFIRE
body: Solvency is about whether **your plan** works. The NEG didn't talk about your plan at all — they talked about what's **already happening** without it. That's `inherency`.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ MISFIRE — RECALIBRATE
body: The clue is *"already phasing out."* When the NEG says the status quo is **already moving** to solve the problem, they're attacking `inherency` — the barrier you claimed exists.

prompt.label: BLUEPRINT REVIEW
prompt.scenario: A cadet stands up to give a 1AC. They talk for five minutes about how terrible plastic pollution is — statistics, stories, photos of beaches covered in trash. They sit down. They never proposed a specific policy.
prompt.question: What's the biggest problem with this Affirmative case?

options.text: Nothing — proving harms is enough on its own
There's no `plan`, so there's no `solvency`. The case is incomplete.
They needed more statistics about pollution
They should have debated the Negative side instead

correct.title: ✓ TARGET ACQUIRED
body: Right. Without a `plan`, the cadet is just **complaining about a problem**. They've established harms, maybe significance — but `solvency` is impossible to prove because there's no specific solution to test.
*"A winning Commander always brings a blueprint."* No blueprint, no win.
correct.followup: Every Affirmative case needs Agent, Action, Funding, Timeline. Memorize those four.

a.title: ✕ MISFIRE
body: Harms alone don't win debates. Even if every harm is real and massive, the NEG just has to ask *"so what do you want us to **do** about it?"* and you'll have no answer.

c.title: ✕ MISFIRE
body: More stats wouldn't fix it. Even a 20-minute speech full of pollution data is still missing the `plan` — the specific policy proposal that lets you argue `solvency`.

d.title: ✕ MISFIRE
body: The cadet's side isn't the issue — the **missing plan** is. An Affirmative case without a plan fails *no matter which side they were assigned*.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ MISFIRE — RECALIBRATE
body: Without a specific policy proposal, you can't prove `solvency` — there's nothing concrete to defend. Every Affirmative case needs a `plan`.

prompt.label: BUILD THE PLAN
prompt.scenario: Every Affirmative `plan` answers four questions. Drop the right term into each blank.
prompt.question: Complete the blueprint.

slides.template: The {{1}} is **who** carries out the plan. The {{2}} is **what** they actually do. The {{3}} is **how** the plan is paid for. The {{4}} is **when** the plan starts.

correct.title: ✓ BLUEPRINT ARMED
body: **Agent · Action · Funding · Timeline.** That's the whole blueprint.
Every time you write a 1AC plan text, run through those four. Miss one, and the NEG has a free shot at your `solvency`.
correct.followup: Pro tip: write your plan **before** you write the rest of your case. Everything else builds on it.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ MISFIRE — RECALIBRATE
body: The four parts of a plan are **Agent** (who), **Action** (what), **Funding** (how), and **Timeline** (when). Try the matching again.

slides.headline: MISSION COMPLETE — AFF CORE ARMED
slides.subtext: You've got the Affirmative burden locked in. S.H.I.S. + a Plan. The Stock Issues sector opens up — Inherency is next.
